day-29-act-01.title: Train, validation, and test: fixing the comparison
day-29-act-01.objective: Explain the role of train/validation/test splits in evaluation and why the test set is read once; fix the evaluation protocol before any tuning begins.
day-29-act-01.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-29-act-01.instructions: Evaluation answers 'does it generalize?' using data the model never trained on. The training split fits parameters; the validation split guides choices (which model, which settings); the test split is the final, untouched read. With 1,000 examples a 60/20/20 split gives 600 train, 200 validation, 200 test. Comparisons are only valid when every candidate is scored on the same split with the same metric — fix that protocol before tuning, not after seeing results.
day-29-act-01.exercise_prompt: A learner has 1,000 labeled examples. (a) Allocate train/validation/test at 60/20/20. (b) Model M1 was selected after 40 trials scored on the test set — name the protocol violation and its consequence. (c) State what must be identical before M1 and M2 scores can be compared.
day-29-act-01.hint: Repeated test reads turn 'test' into validation — the reported number becomes optimistically biased. Before comparing: same held-out data, same metric, same preprocessing.
day-29-act-01.answer: (a) 600 train, 200 validation, 200 test. (b) The test set was reused for model selection, so the reported score is biased upward — the violation is selection on the test set; fix by selecting on validation and reading test once. (c) Same test split, same metric, same preprocessing and evaluation code; otherwise the difference is uninterpretable.
day-29-act-01.mastery_criterion: Learner states each split's role in evaluation, names the test-reuse violation, and writes the fixed-protocol checklist before any tuning.

day-29-act-02.title: Baselines and data leakage
day-29-act-02.prerequisites: Activity 29-01; no AI assistance in this block.
day-29-act-02.objective: Compute a trivial baseline and detect at least two leakage mechanisms that make an evaluation report a fabricated success.
day-29-act-02.instructions: A baseline is the cheapest honest predictor: for classification, the majority class. If 900 of 1,000 examples are class 0, always predicting class 0 scores 0.90 — any model is judged against 0.90, not 0.0. Leakage is information flowing from evaluation data into training: normalization statistics computed on all rows before splitting, duplicated rows crossing the split, or a feature derived from the label. Each inflates the evaluation without real skill.
day-29-act-02.exercise_prompt: (a) Dataset: 1,000 examples, 900 in class 0 — what is the majority baseline? A model reports 0.92: what is the real improvement? (b) A pipeline standardizes features using the mean of all 1,000 rows, then splits 60/20/20 — is the 0.92 score trustworthy, and why? (c) 50 test rows also appear (duplicated) inside the 600-row training set — what happens to the evaluation?
day-29-act-02.hint: Baseline = 0.90, so the true lift is 0.02. Statistics fitted on all data leak distributional information; duplicated rows let the model memorize evaluation inputs.
day-29-act-02.answer: (a) Baseline 0.90; real improvement 0.92 − 0.90 = 0.02. (b) Not fully trustworthy: fitting the scaler on all data leaks validation/test statistics into preprocessing — fit preprocessing parameters on the training split only. (c) Duplicates let the model memorize test answers, inflating the score — deduplicate before splitting; the honest report is the lower, leakage-free number, not the fabricated 0.92.
day-29-act-02.mastery_criterion: Baseline computed, at least two leakage mechanisms named with the correct fixes (fit-on-train-only, deduplicate, drop label-derived features), and the learner reports the honest lower number rather than the inflated one.

day-29-act-03.title: Metrics and distribution shift
day-29-act-03.objective: Read accuracy, cross-entropy loss, and perplexity as the same evaluation evidence at different resolutions, and diagnose a score drop caused by distribution shift rather than model failure.
day-29-act-03.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-29-act-03.instructions: Accuracy counts right answers; cross-entropy (the mean −ln p assigned to the correct label) also prices confidence — p = 0.9 costs 0.105, p = 0.5 costs 0.693, p = 0.1 costs 2.303. Perplexity is exp(mean cross-entropy): the effective number of equally likely choices — a model always assigning p = 0.5 to the right token has perplexity 2, and a uniform guesser over 4 options has perplexity 4. Distribution shift breaks the train≈test assumption: a detector trained on daytime photos evaluated at night faces a new evaluation of a new distribution, not automatically a model defect.
day-29-act-03.exercise_prompt: (a) For correct-label probabilities [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6], compute the mean cross-entropy and the perplexity. (b) A model scores 18/20 = 0.90 accuracy on its test split but 11/20 on night-time photos — give two distinct explanations and the follow-up check for each. (c) Which perplexity is better, 2.0 or 10.0, and what does each mean?
day-29-act-03.hint: Mean NLL = (0.105+0.223+0.357+0.511)/4 ≈ 0.299; perplexity = e^0.299 ≈ 1.35. Shift explanations: the night set is genuinely harder (new distribution) vs. a preprocessing mismatch. Perplexity is a branching factor — lower is better, floor is 1.
day-29-act-03.answer: (a) Mean NLL ≈ 0.2990, perplexity = e^0.2990 ≈ 1.35. (b) Shift explanation: inputs moved off the training distribution — collect night examples and re-split honestly. Preprocessing explanation: normalization or label mapping differs at eval time — diff the pipelines. The follow-up check is the same: evaluate on a matched-distribution held-out set. (c) Perplexity 2.0 is better — the model behaves like choosing among ~2 options vs ~10; the floor is 1.0, and a uniform guesser over the vocabulary has perplexity = vocabulary size.
day-29-act-03.mastery_criterion: Correct NLL/perplexity arithmetic, the accuracy-vs-loss distinction stated, and shift versus defect separated with a concrete check for each.

day-29-act-04.title: Assessment: design a valid small experiment
day-29-act-04.objective: Design a complete, honest evaluation for a tiny classification task and defend every choice.
day-29-act-04.instructions: Scenario: 800 labeled examples, two candidate models, classes split 80/20. Design the evaluation end to end and write it as a protocol: splits with sizes, baseline, primary metric plus one supporting metric, leakage checks, when the test set is read, and how you would report a negative result. Work without AI assistance; the point is a defensible protocol, not a lucky number.
day-29-act-04.exercise_prompt: Write the protocol for the 800-example task (suggested 480/160/160), including the majority baseline value, the metric you would report besides accuracy, the three leakage checks, and the sentence you would write if the fancy model only matches the baseline.
day-29-act-04.hint: Baseline = 0.80. Leakage checks: preprocessing fit on train only, no duplicates across splits, no label-derived features. Report mean NLL or a per-class score besides accuracy. A tie with the baseline is a negative result — report it.
day-29-act-04.answer: Reference protocol: 480 train / 160 validation / 160 test; majority baseline 0.80; report accuracy plus mean cross-entropy (or per-class recall); checks — scaler and vocabulary fitted on train only, deduplicated across splits, no feature derived from the label; test read once after validation selects the model; honest sentence: 'model B matched the 0.80 baseline within noise, so it provides no demonstrated improvement' — a negative result reported, not hidden.
day-29-act-04.mastery_criterion: Protocol is complete and internally consistent, states baseline 0.80 and at least one non-accuracy metric, includes the three leakage checks and the single test read, and the negative-result sentence is written without euphemism.
